tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: HIV Testing Services > Summary of Changes
tables.caption: Chapter 3 HIV testing services: summary of changes, 2022 vs 2024 guidance
tables.caption_note: Printed heading 'SUMMARY OF CHANGES'; table continues onto p.9.

body.t: Training of HTS counsellors to be conducted by PSI and TASC
Any accredited institution recognized by SNAP and EHLS may train HTS Counsellors. Entry requirements for HTS training is completion of Form V.
The HIV testing screening tool will be used to determine eligibility for HTS.

HIVST replaces the risk based HTS screening tool in all individuals 12 years and above (excluding clients eligible for routine testing). Routine testing following the National HIV Testing Algorithm should be offered to malnourished and sick children, HIV-exposed children, clients with confirmed or presumptive TB disease, STI clients, index contacts and inpatient, pregnant and lactating women and KPs.
Use the HIV screening tool for children and adolescents (6-15yrs) to determine eligibility for HTS.
All children 2-11 years utilize the paediatric HIV screening tool in all entry points unless they qualify for routine testing.

HIV Self-test kits/Oraquick can be distributed at the health facility level and performed privately in the client's home or facilitated by a healthcare worker in a private setting at a health facility.
The age of consent for HIVST has been reduced from 16 years to 12 years.
Frequency of rescreening for HIV undefined

For children 2-11 years rescreen at every encounter using the risk assessment tool. For all individuals 12 years and above rescreen at every facility encounter using HIVST. For ANC and PMTCT, retesting guidelines remain unchanged (refer to Eswatini Integrated HIV Management Guidelines 2022, Chapter 3). For all clients eligible for routine testing, retesting guidelines remain unchanged (refer to the 2022 Guidelines, Chapter 3). PrEP retesting guidelines remain unchanged (refer to the 2022 Guidelines, Chapter 3).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: HIV Testing Services > 3.2 HIV Screening Tools > HIV eligibility screening process flow
tables.caption: Figure 3.1 The HIV eligibility screening process flow
tables.content:
Applies to all clients presenting in the facility or community, EXCEPT clients eligible for routine testing (malnourished and sick children, HIV-exposed children, clients with confirmed or presumptive TB disease, STI clients, index contacts, pregnant and lactating mothers, inpatients and key populations).

1. Patient arrives. Ask: ever tested for HIV?
  - NO: Refer to HTS counsellor for: risk assessment for children 2-11 years; HIVST screening for children 12 years and above, adolescents and adults. Then the patient may proceed to the consultation room.
  - YES: ask: what is your status?
      - Negative: Refer to HTS counsellor for: risk assessment for children 2-11 years; HIVST screening for children 12 years and above, adolescents and adults. Then the patient may proceed to the consultation room.
      - Positive: on ART?
          - NO: refer for ART initiation & LCM, then the patient may proceed to the consultation room.
          - YES: the patient may proceed to the consultation room.
2. Patient exits.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 3: HIV Testing Services > 3.2 HIV Screening Tools > 3.2.2.1 Use of HIV-ST Among All Individuals 12 Years & Above > Use of HIV-ST among PrEP clients
tables.caption: Use of HIV-ST among PrEP clients
tables.content:
There are two key approaches where HIVST can be considered as part of PrEP delivery:
1. Demand generation and linkage to PrEP: HIVST can be an important tool to generate demand for PrEP by reaching individuals who may not otherwise test or access health facilities.
2. PrEP (re-)initiation and follow-up visits: HIVST can be used for clients (re-)initiating or continuing oral PrEP or the PrEP ring. For CAB-LA users, a National HIV Testing Algorithm needs to be used.

body.t: At one month, then every three months.
At one month, then every two months.
HIVST for all clients except PBFW who will receive a National HIV Testing Algorithm during their ANC/PNC visit.

At the first follow-up visit (M1), oral PrEP/PrEP ring can be dispensed for a maximum of three months. For the second refill (M4), the PrEP method can be dispensed for a maximum of six months if the client meets ALL of the following criteria: (a) attending the FU appointment on time (within 7 days of scheduled visit date); (b) does not report any side-effects; (c) wants to continue with the same PrEP method; (d) is not pregnant or breastfeeding or has any comorbidities [as printed]; (e) is willing to take an HIVST after three months, and if HIV negative continues with the remaining three months of PrEP, or if positive discontinues the PrEP method and reports to the facility for confirmation of the test result and linkage to ART. For clients not meeting the above criteria, a maximum refill of three months can be done at any time.
After initiation injection 1 and 2, re-injections will be given every 2 months (+/- 7 days).
Clients eligible and receiving 6MMD should be provided with an HIVST to test after using 3 months of their PrEP product. For ED PrEP clients, consider providing 2 HIVST for any in between exposure.
3 or 6 months depending if client qualifies for 6MMD and available stock. For PBFW clients, PrEP visits should be aligned with ANC and PNC visits.
After initiation injection 2, follow up appointments and re-injection will be every 2 months.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 4: Referral & Linkages > Summary of Changes
tables.caption: Chapter 4 referral and linkages: summary of changes, 2022 vs 2024 guidance

body.t: Referral and linkages to prevention or care and treatment services should be provided to both negative and positive clients, respectively.

The old guidance is unchanged. However, providers should shift to implementing a status neutral approach: all individuals provided with HTS should be directly linked to services appropriate to their health needs (prevention or ART services) regardless of HIV status.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 4: Referral & Linkages > 4.1 Status Neutral Approach > Status-neutral HIV prevention and care
tables.caption: Status-Neutral HIV Prevention and Care (diagram)
tables.content:
Everyone starts with an HIV test; services are linked to the result, regardless of HIV status.

- HIV test negative: Prevention pathway (prevents getting HIV). People whose HIV tests are negative are offered powerful prevention tools like PrEP, condoms, harm reduction (e.g., SSPs), and supportive services to stay HIV negative. Supported by HIV and STD testing and high-impact HIV prevention.
- HIV test positive: Treatment pathway (prevents transmitting HIV). People whose HIV tests are positive enter primary care and are offered effective treatment and supportive services to achieve and maintain viral suppression. Supported by HIV primary care and effective treatment.
- People newly diagnosed with HIV move from the prevention pathway to the treatment pathway.
- Across both pathways: quality care; culturally inclusive and responsive quality care; prevent and treat syndemic infections.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 5: Basic Care Package for HIV-Positive Individuals > Summary of Changes
tables.caption: Chapter 5 basic care package: summary of changes in viral load testing, MMD and HIVDR, 2022 vs 2024 guidance

body.t: Pretreatment VL for all newly diagnosed clients initiating ART. Clients returning to care should not receive PTVL.
The first routine VL test is to be done by 6 months post-ART initiation.
The first routine VL test is to be done 3 months post-ART initiation. Ensure that all clients have a VL test done BY 6 months of starting ART.
The 2nd routine VL test should be done 6 months after an initial suppressed VL test result.

The 2nd routine VL test should be done 6 months after an initial suppressed VL test result and then annually thereafter. For children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, it should be done every 6 months.
3MMD can be started after a suppressed VL done 6 months following ART initiation.
Up to 3MMD of ARVs can be started after an initial suppressed VL test result done at 3 months. Up to 6MMD can be given following 2 consecutive suppressed VL test results.
Remnant blood samples of all infants who test HIV positive may be stored and used for surveillance purposes (plasma or DBS) for HIVDR survey activities.
Routine HIVDR testing for all PrEP breakthrough infections.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 5: Basic Care Package for HIV-Positive Individuals > 5.3 HIV Care Escalation Plan > National client escalation plan
tables.caption: Figure 5.1 National Client Escalation Plan for HIV care (steps from HTS counsellor to clinical psychologist)
tables.content:
Clients are escalated step by step to the next level of care. Feedback is received from every level of care for quality documentation purposes.

Step 1 - HTS counsellor: identification of all positives pending linkage; provides motivational counselling and refers to the expert client (EC) as client role model to provide context.

Step 2 - Expert client (EC):
  - Newly diagnosed: motivates clients to start early using practical life experiences as examples.
  - Clients already on ART: EC identifies clients struggling with adherence and barriers at refill, pill count, missed appointment/defaulter, IIT and HVL level. Provides counselling based on stage and escalates the client.

Step 3 - Nurses and doctors: confirm the barrier identified by the EC or counsellor; explore other barriers missed; provide further motivational counselling; identify the category of barrier and escalate based on criterion:
  - Social barriers: escalate to social worker.
  - Cognitive, behavioural & emotional: escalate to psychologist.
  - Community follow-up and care: escalate to APS Associate & CEC.

Step 4 - Clinical social workers: conduct one-on-one sessions with clients; if need be, conduct home visits, home assessments etc.; assess clients' needs, situations, strengths and support networks to determine their goals; help clients adjust to changes and challenges in their lives; provide motivational counselling; escalate the client to the psychologist or any other HCW for further care.

Step 5 - Clinical psychologist: participate in MDT-SUAC sessions and one-on-one sessions to identify cognitive, emotional & behavioural barriers; understand clients' needs, assess attitude, behaviour and abilities; diagnose psychological, emotional or behavioural disorders; work with nurses, social workers and EC to help the client resolve issues identified.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 5: Basic Care Package for HIV-Positive Individuals > 5.3 HIV Care Escalation Plan > Indications for the HIV care escalation plan
tables.caption: Figure 5.2 Clients eligible for the HIV care escalation plan
tables.content:
HCWs are encouraged to escalate (refer) any clients they experience difficulties in managing, including those below. Management of such patients requires a multidisciplinary team (MDT) approach. Referrals can also be made for specialised services, e.g. psychiatrists, physicians, paediatricians.

Clients eligible for the HIV care escalation plan:
- Newly diagnosed
- Delayed ART initiation
- Clients with AHD, NCDs and other complicated conditions
- Clients with high viral load
- Caregiver (refusing child initiation, poor adherence in child)
- Returning to care (re-engaging)
- Clients with very poor social circumstances

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > Summary of Changes > Updated viral load thresholds
tables.caption: Figure 7.1 Updated viral load thresholds
tables.content:
Following ART initiation, a VL decline of at least 0.5 log10 copies/mL (3-fold) is considered significant. The goal for people on ART is an undetectable VL (VL <50 copies/mL). To keep community transmission to a minimum, the threshold for viral suppression has been decreased to VL <200 copies/mL.

Viral load categories:
- Undetectable viral load: VL <50 copies/mL
- Viral suppression: VL <200 copies/mL
- Low-level viraemia: VL 50-999 copies/mL
- High viral load: VL >1000 copies/mL

Undetectable and suppressed: U = U (undetectable = untransmittable). Low-level viraemia and high viral load: high predictor of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR).
PTVL as part of baseline laboratory tests should not be done for clients re-engaging into care.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.1 Routine VL Monitoring > Updated viral load monitoring schedule
tables.caption: Figure 7.2 Updated viral load monitoring schedule
tables.content:
All clients initiating or reinitiating ART should receive their first routine VL three months after (re)initiating ART and at 9 months thereafter. After two consecutive undetectable VL results, routine VL testing is done as below.

Schedule: pre-treatment VL, then VL at 3 months post ART initiation, then VL at 9 months post ART, then routine VL testing.

Routine VL testing frequency:
- Children and adolescents (0-19 years): every 6 months
- Pregnant and breastfeeding women: every 6 months
- 3rd line clients: every 6 months
- Adults >19 years: annually

tables.heading_path: Chapter 7: Adult Antiretroviral Therapy > 7.1 Routine VL Monitoring > Viral load testing algorithm
tables.caption: Figure 7.3 The viral load testing algorithm (ART-naive vs treatment-experienced)
tables.content:
The management of HVL remains the same.

Start: client presents for HTS. Verify if they are a true new positive.

Path A - ART naive: baseline laboratory tests INCLUDING PTVL; ART initiation.
  At 3 months post ART initiation:
  - VL <200 copies/ml: eligible for up to 3MMD. At 9 months post ART initiation, VL <200 copies/ml: eligible for MMD & DSD enrolment; routine VL monitoring thereafter.
  - VL >200 copies/ml: SUAC. Then: VL >200 copies/ml*: see management of LLV*; VL <200 copies/ml*: eligible for MMD.

Path B - treatment experienced: baseline laboratory tests EXCLUDING PTVL; re-initiate on previous regimen.
  At 3 months:
  - VL <200 copies/ml: continue current ART regimen; eligible for up to 3MMD. At 9 months, VL <200 copies/ml: eligible for up to 6MMD & DSD enrolment; routine VL monitoring thereafter.
  - VL >200 copies/ml: SUAC. Then: VL <200 copies/ml: eligible for up to 6MMD & DSD enrolment, routine VL monitoring thereafter; VL >200 copies/ml*: see management of LLV*.

Notes printed under the figure:
(a) If VL 200-999 copies/ml, follow management of LLV.
(b) If VL > 1000 copies/ml, start SUAC.
(c) Repeat VL after 3 months and consult the clinical advisor of HIVDR for persistent low-level viraemia.
All clients with a detectable viral load should be closely monitored with adherence support until they are undetectable.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission of HIV > Same Day Management of Viraemia in Pregnant Women
tables.caption: Figure 8.1 Same day management of viraemia in pregnant women (flowchart)
tables.content:
Starting point: pregnant woman with VL > 50 c/mL.

Path A - VL 50-1000 c/mL AND on DTG for less than 18 months (DTG <18/12):
Intensive adherence interventions:
  1. DOT
  2. Mentor mother/EC involvement
  3. Follow-up VL after 1 month (F/U VL 1/12)
  4. If VL remains >1000, or VL remains 50-1000, consult the DR committee

Path B - on DTG for more than 18 months, or duration unknown (DTG >18/12 or unknown):
Step 1. Genotype if VL > 1000*. Send genotypes the same day (unless known default or very poor adherence in the first trimester). Complete and submit a genotype motivation to snapthirdline@mohcoag.org.
Step 2. Then by timing of the detectable viral load (DVL):
  - 1st DVL in the 1st or 2nd trimester: intensive adherence interventions as in Path A.
  - 1st DVL in the 3rd trimester, OR 2nd DVL in any trimester: Empiric therapy, chosen by prior PI use:
  - No prior PI: TLD 1 tab OD PLUS EITHER DRV/r (400/50) 2 tabs OD* OR ATV/r (300/50) 1 tab OD (*if available)
  - Prior PI: TLD 1 tab OD PLUS DRV/r (600/100) BD
  Provide the same intensive adherence interventions as in Path A.

When the baby is born:
  - 2 drug EIP x 6 weeks (X6/52) and then NVP only, minimum 14 weeks (14/52), and mother is documented undetectable.
  - Consider 3 drug ART for babies born to women with seroconversion at delivery; perform 2 tests prior to initiation.
  - VL at delivery for all women.
  - Birth test all infants.
  - Please consult for PLW with viraemia on concurrent ATT.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission of HIV > Summary of Changes
tables.caption: Chapter 8 PMTCT: summary of changes (viraemia in pregnant/breastfeeding women, infant PEP, DR committee), 2022 vs 2024 guidance

body.t: Genotypes were recommended for pregnant or breastfeeding women failing a DTG or PI based ART regimen.

Updated guidance provides more details for same day clinical care decisions and consideration of empiric therapy for women deemed highest risk while awaiting genotype results. Emphasis is placed on intensive adherence interventions for all women with a DVL >50.
No specific recommendations for breastfeeding infants of mothers found to have seroconverted.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 8: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission of HIV > Same Day Management of Viraemia in Breastfeeding Women
tables.caption: Figure 8.2 Same day management of viraemia in breastfeeding women (flowchart)
tables.content:
First: test the infant immediately. If reactive, initiate ART as soon as possible. If non-reactive, follow the algorithm below. Consider presumptive ART in all HIV-exposed infants (HEI) who appear ill/FTT while awaiting test results.

Starting point: breastfeeding woman with viraemia.

Path A - VL 50-1000 c/mL AND on DTG for less than 18 months (printed: 'TLD1 and TLD2 DTG <18/12'):
Intensive adherence interventions:
  1. DOT
  2. Mentor mother/EC involvement
  3. Follow-up VL after 1 month (F/U VL 1/12)
  4. If VL remains >1000, or VL remains 50-1000, consult the DR committee

Path B - on DTG for more than 18 months, or duration unknown (printed: 'TLD1 and TLD2 on DTG > 18/12 or unknown'):
Step 1. Genotype if VL > 1000*. Send genotypes the same day (unless known default or very poor adherence in the first trimester). Complete and submit a genotype motivation to snapthirdline@mohcoag.org.
Step 2. Then:
  - 1st DVL: intensive adherence interventions as in Path A.
  - 2nd DVL: discuss AFASS; if breastfeeding is ongoing, proceed to Empiric therapy, chosen by prior PI use:
  - No prior PI: TLD 1 tab OD PLUS EITHER DRV/r (400/50) 2 tabs OD* OR ATV/r (300/50) 1 tab OD (*if available)
  - Prior PI: TLD 1 tab OD PLUS DRV/r (600/100) BD
  Provide the same intensive adherence interventions as in Path A.

Caring for the breastfeeding child:
  - If child is <6 weeks (<6/52): continue EIP (AZT/NVP; printed 'AT/NVP').
  - If child is >6 weeks (>6/52): continue or restart NVP until the mother is undetectable.
  - If AFASS criteria are met and the mother prefers to wean after clear discussion of risks and benefits, advise weaning.
  - Follow a weaned infant monthly for weight check.
  - If the mother acutely seroconverted, test the infant. If negative, consider PEP in the baby until the mother is undetectable.

body.section: Children initiating TB treatment while on ART

body.t: Increase DTG [note 2] to twice daily dosing. Continue current backbone.

*Maintain all dose adjustments for 2 weeks after completion of ATT. *The preferred regimen for children with DTG resistance is an optimized NRTI backbone with LPV/r [note 3]. If this is not available a holding regimen of AZT/3TC/ABC OR NNRTI based therapy may be necessary. Please consult with an expert in Paediatric HIV/TB.

Preferred: If DTG-naïve, transition to a DTG [note 2]-based regimen (with appropriate dose adjustment). Continue current backbone. Alternative: If DTG is not possible, LPV/r [note 3] dose adjustment is needed: Ritonavir (RTV) dose needs to be "super-boosted" to achieve the same dose as LPV in mg, in a ratio equal to or approaching 1:1. In older children and adolescents swallowing tablets the LPV/r dose can be doubled.
Change of regimen is needed: replace DRV/r with DTG [note 2] if DTG-naive or with LPV/r [note 3] if DTG-experienced (with appropriate dose adjustment). Continue current backbone.
Change of regimen is needed: replace ATV/r with DTG if DTG-naive or with LPV/r [note 3] if DTG-experienced (with appropriate dose adjustment). Continue current backbone.

body.section: Neonates (first 28 days of life) initiating TB treatment while on ART

body.t: Change of regimen is needed: substitute NVP as soon as possible with DTG [note 2] or LPV/r [note 3] (with appropriate dose adjustment).

footnotes: [note 1] Do not use lead in dosing and use the maximum recommended dose by neonatal dosing chart if administering with rifampicin. Transition to DTG when 3 kgs and 4 weeks of age.
[note 2] DTG should be dosed twice daily in children on TB treatment. This dose adjustment must continue for 2 weeks after completing ATT.

[note 3] If used, LPV/r dose adjustment is needed: ritonavir (RTV) dose needs to be "super-boosted" to achieve the same dose as LPV in mg, in a ratio equal to or approaching 1:1. In older children and adolescents swallowing tablets the LPV/r dose can be doubled. This dose adjustment must continue for 2 weeks after completing ATT.

body.t: ABC + 3TC + DTG [note 2]; TDF + 3TC + LPV/r [note 3]; ABC + 3TC + LPV/r [note 3]

footnotes: [note 1] Do not use lead in dosing; use the maximum recommended dose by neonatal dosing chart if administering with rifampicin. Transition to DTG when 3 kgs and 4 weeks of age.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 9: ART for Children & Adolescents > 9.5 Clinical Monitoring of Children & Adolescents on ART > ART follow-up schedule and MMD eligibility
tables.caption: Figure 9.4 Key ART follow-up schedule for children and adolescents starting ART and MMD eligibility
tables.content:
Ensure weight-band dose adjustments when refilling paediatric clients' ART.

- ART initiation: follow up 2 weeks and 1 month after initiation. First VL at 3 months. Monthly refills.
- >1 year old (on ART): if undetectable viral load x2 and clinically stable [note 1], may space to 3-month refills.
- >2 years old (on ART): if undetectable viral load x1 and clinically stable [note 1], may space to 3-month refills. When undetectable viral load x2 and clinically stable [note 1], may space to 6-month refills.

[note 1] Although children younger than 5 years are defined as having Advanced HIV Disease at presentation, those who have been receiving ART >1 year and who are clinically stable (reliable caregiver, undetectable viral load, no OIs, normal growth curve, normal development, appropriately immunized for age, stable vital signs) should not be considered to have advanced disease and should be eligible/have the option for multi-month dispensing. Multi-month (MMD) refills should include prophylaxis (CTX, TPT). Family-centred care should be implemented, and ART care appointments for the mother and their babies should be linked to the mother-baby pair visit schedules. Caregiver literacy is emphasised to ensure adherence and retention in care.

Baseline and 3-month VL tests are additional tests; this aligns with the CWF visits and supports service integration. VL testing should routinely be done at 0, 3, 9 and 15 months and thereafter every 6 months.

Tests at each time point:
- ART initiation: CD4 and VL
- 3 months: VL
- 6 months: CD4
- 9 months: VL
- 12 months: CD4
- 15 months: VL
- Every 6 months thereafter: VL

tables.heading_path: Chapter 10: HIV/NCDs & Mental Health > 10.1 Psychological Care & Support > Screening for common psychological disorders & social issues
tables.caption: Figure 10.1 Psycho-social (PSS) Risk Assessment Screening Tool score chart
tables.content:
Every client seen by an HCW must be screened for common psychological disorders and social issues (depression, suicide, anxiety, substance use, social issues) using the Psychosocial Risk Assessment Screening Tool, then provided Psychological First Aid (PFA) and referred to a psychologist or social worker.

Action by area (as printed in the chart):
- Depression: if the client responded yes or sometimes, provide PFA then refer to psychologist.
- Suicide: same.
- Anxiety: same.
- Substance use: same.
- Social issues: same (chart says refer to psychologist).

Scoring rules printed below the chart:
- 'Yes' or 'sometimes' for questions 1-10: provide PFA and refer to psychologist.
- 'Yes' or 'sometimes' for questions 11-15: provide PFA and refer to clinical social worker.
- 'No': continue with SUAC.

Any client who answers YES to suicidal ideation should be further assessed and admitted if they are at risk of self-harm.
source_flags: Image in the PDF; transcribed from the page image.
The chart sends social issues to the psychologist, while the rule below sends questions 11-15 to the clinical social worker. Possible inconsistency in the source; clinician to confirm.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 10: HIV/NCDs & Mental Health > 10.1 Psychological Care & Support > Depression screening (PHQ-9)
tables.caption: Figure 10.2 Depression screening using PHQ-9 score chart
tables.content:
PHQ-9 score: severity and action
- 0-4: no or minimal depression. Action: none.
- 5-9: mild depression. Action: monitor and repeat PHQ-9 after 2 weeks to 3 months depending on symptom severity.
- 10-14: moderate depression. Action: counselling + pharmacotherapy.
- 15-19: moderately severe depression. Action: psychotherapy + pharmacotherapy.
- 20-27: severe depression. Action: start pharmacotherapy and refer immediately to the National Psychiatric Hospital.

If a client scores 10 and above, they must be given psychotherapy as indicated in Section 5.9.2 of the 2022 Integrated HIV Management Guidelines and Annex 11.24.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 10: HIV/NCDs & Mental Health > 10.1 Psychological Care & Support > Suicide screening
tables.caption: Figure 10.3 Suicide screening using Suicide Risk Assessment Tool score chart
tables.content:
Suicide Risk Assessment Tool score: risk and management
- 0-10: low. Provide psychotherapy and refer for psychiatric services.
- 11-20: medium. Provide psychotherapy and refer for psychiatric services.
- 20-30: high. Refer to psychiatric centre / involuntary admission.

Provide psychotherapy or refer. Rule out mental disorders such as major depressive disorder and manage as indicated (Mental Health Desk Guide, 2022).

tables.heading_path: Chapter 10: HIV/NCDs & Mental Health > 10.1 Psychological Care & Support > Anxiety screening (BAI)
tables.caption: Figure 10.4 Anxiety screening using Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI)
tables.content:
BAI score: level and management
- 0-21: low anxiety. Provide Psychological First Aid; refer to doctor-led services every 6 months for review.
- 22-35: moderate anxiety. Psychotherapy; refer to psychiatric services.
- 36+: potentially concerning level of anxiety. Psychotherapy; refer to psychiatric services.

Refer to the clinical psychologist for psychotherapy if there is no improvement with counselling (Mental Health Desk Guide, 2022).
source_flags: Image in the PDF; transcribed from the page image.

tables.heading_path: Chapter 10: HIV/NCDs & Mental Health > 10.1 Psychological Care & Support > Substance use screening (ASSIST)
tables.caption: Figure 10.5 Substance use screening using ASSIST screening tool
tables.content:
ASSIST score: risk and management
- 0-3: low. Brief education: inform patients about the risks of illicit drug use and signs of substance use disorder.
- 4-26: moderate. Brief intervention: motivational interviewing to raise patients' awareness of their substance use; refer to psychiatric services.
- 27+: severe. Brief intervention: psychotherapy and refer to psychiatric services.

Carefully assess for drug use patterns and related physical, psychological and social issues contributing to substance use behaviour (Mental Health Desk Guide, 2022).

## CHAPTER 3: HIV TESTING SERVICES

### INTRODUCTION

Even though Eswatini has made tremendous progress towards HIV Epidemic Control, findings from SHIMS3 (2021) indicate that critical case-finding gaps remain at the sub-population level among children 15 years and below, women 15-29 years, men 25-34 years, the military and key populations (MSM & FSW). These HTS gaps need to be addressed to ensure Eswatini fully achieves and maintains the first 95 UNAIDS HIV epidemic control target.

### **PURPOSE**

This addendum seeks to provide guidance to address current HTS gaps through strategic shifts in HTS implementation, and adoption of a status-neutral approach as the key gateway for entry into care.
